name: Tara Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential. What happens on a normal building-site day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am fifty-eight and lead a crew fitting large timber roof panels on building sites. My trade certificate got me started; now people call me when a lift needs a careful plan and a second check. I use AI every day to compare the panel list with the drawing, but I inspect the slings and landing point myself. My partner and I have grown children, a good wage and more than six months of expenses saved; I hope to leave regular site work at sixty-six in 2034 if the household income covers it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that a faster list is welcome, but the lift still needs a person looking at the sling. An AI roof-panel count cannot see a frayed sling above a building site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect our fitting work and my higher wage to carry on. We have over six months saved and plenty of nearby construction firms, so a small office change does not threaten the household.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading safe roof-panel lifts and use the AI list comparison I already know. I would check slings before each lift and review our age-sixty-six retirement income with my partner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about paid work here. The budget review is ordinary planning, not a decision to leave early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a sling check involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I look for fraying, the tag and the correct attachment points before the panel leaves the ground. Then a second worker watches the landing area.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you call the list check a new AI skill?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I already use it daily. A new skill would mean learning a new control, not repeating the same morning comparison.

say: I would **use** AI for panel counts and check every lift physically.
I would **tell** the crew that a sling has to pass inspection before lifting.
think: My **higher** pay and strong savings make the plateau secure.
**Retirement** at sixty-six still depends on actual income and expenses.
do: **Keep** leading roof-panel lifts and checking sling attachments.
**Review** expected age-sixty-six retirement income against our housing, food and repair costs with my partner.
feel: **Calm** about safe paid work and familiar daily AI use.
S0.quote: An AI roof-panel count cannot see a frayed sling above a building site.
fieldNote: **Tara** uses AI daily for panel lists but treats slings and landing areas as physical safety decisions.
**Higher** pay, more than six months saved and many nearby builders make a small AI change manageable.

steps.text: Keep leading and checking building-site roof-panel lifts
Review age-sixty-six retirement budget before deciding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An AI roof lift schedule cannot make an unpaid sling inspection safe. I would learn a new AI lift-sequencing control early and take the time records to our union site meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can see the builder compressing the paid preparation between lifts. My own overtime might shrink, even though our savings protect the household for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would practise the new control on a completed lift plan and compare it with two live lifts. I would keep paid panel shifts and ask the union representative to secure written paid inspection and stop-lift time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about possible paid-hour loss but interested in the tool. A faster schedule is only useful if nobody is rushed past a safety check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would fail your lift-sequencing test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A plan that puts the next panel in the air before the landing zone is clear. I would stop the lift and show the actual site record.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the union to write down?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paid time to inspect slings and stop an unsafe lift without losing wages. I would bring the recorded preparation minutes to the meeting.

I would **ask** the union for paid sling checks and stop-lift time.
think: My **overtime** could shrink under tighter schedules.
**Strong** savings let me negotiate, but they do not make rushed lifting safe.
do: **Practise** new AI sequencing control on completed and live roof lifts.
**Keep** paid panel shifts while recording inspection minutes.
**Seek** union clause for paid sling inspection and stop-lift authority.
feel: **Anxious** about plausible overtime loss, with means to respond.
S1.quote: An AI roof lift schedule cannot make an unpaid sling inspection safe.
fieldNote: She **practises** a new AI control and checks it against live safety conditions.
Her **union** request is a concrete meeting action over paid inspection time, while her own overtime may realistically shrink.

steps.text: Learn new AI sequencing control on roof-panel lifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew thinking AI can plan roof lifts in 2028 when I am sixty, but hands-on robots arrive around 2031 when I am sixty-three. That is three years before my hoped-for retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A roof robot in 2031 could lift a panel while my paid work and the sling-check duty are both being cut. Our strong savings and many local builders offer choices, yet the income calculation has to cover the years after any early exit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would request a paid supervised trial of robot-guided panel lifting, with a human checking slings and authority to stop an unsafe lift; I would participate only if an offered paid place exists. If hours fall, I would apply to posted local lift-safety jobs only where wages cover our bills and the stop-lift duty is written.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about possible lost fitting hours, but able to test options. I would not retire at sixty-three just because an account holds six months of cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you stop in that trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A lift where the robot’s sling angle differs from the approved plan or workers are in the landing area. I would require a clear zone and a paid human check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the builder has no paid trial place?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stay on my paid roof crew and keep asking for written hours. I would not present a request as if I had already tested a robot.

say: **Thinking** AI changes lift planning in 2028; robots may lift panels around 2031.
I would **request** a paid supervised trial, subject to an offered place.
think: **Paid** panel hours may fall three years before my target.
A **real** local safety role needs adequate wages and written stop-lift authority.
do: **Request** paid supervised robot-lift trial with human sling checks and stop-lift authority.
**Keep** paid roof-panel shifts unless a trial place is offered.
**Apply** after cuts to posted local lift-safety role with adequate pay and stop-lift authority.
feel: **Anxious** about possible own-hour loss, with savings and nearby options.
S2.quote: A roof robot in 2031 could lift a panel while my paid work and the sling-check duty are both being cut.
fieldNote: She **requests** a trial and explicitly waits for an offered paid supervised place before participating.
**Any** fallback application follows actual hour loss and requires a posted local role, household-covering wage and written safety authority.

steps.text: Keep paid roof shifts; request supervised paid robot-sling trial with stop-lift authority
Apply after cuts to posted local lift-safety role with adequate pay and stop-lift authority

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI arrives in 2031 when I am sixty-three, with capable site robots around 2034 when I am sixty-six. If our original age-sixty-six retirement in 2034 is affordable, the physical change meets my planned exit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would still consider formal lifting inspection if income falls short. A lift-safety certificate is just paper if the paid inspector cannot stop a damaged sling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the paid roof crew and check our age-sixty-six household income with my partner. If we need more work and a suitable local lift inspector vacancy is posted, I would complete its fully funded paid-time course and apply after qualifying only if the job pays our bills and includes written stop-lift authority.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy until the budget is checked, but I have time to make a sound choice. I will not pretend an inspection certificate guarantees a place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the course add to your present lift checks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Formal inspection and sign-off of another crew’s rigging, rather than checking my own lift. I would need the proper qualification and written authority.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course is free but the training days are unpaid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stay on the paid crew. A few months of study without wages is not a good offer even with savings.

say: The 2034 **robot** date meets my original retirement target if affordable.
I would **take** formal lift inspection training only if more income is needed.
think: A **posted** local inspector job must pay household bills and carry stop-lift authority.
**Course** funding alone is insufficient without paid study days.
do: **Check** age-sixty-six household income against ongoing costs.
**Enrol** if income falls short in funded paid-time training for a posted local lift-inspector role covering bills.
**Apply** after qualifying to posted local inspector job with adequate pay and stop-lift authority.
feel: **Uneasy** until retirement income and later role terms are verified.
S3.quote: A lift-safety certificate is just paper if the paid inspector cannot stop a damaged sling.
fieldNote: Her **course** enrollment and later application are separate conditional decisions.
The **retirement** target predates the scenario; continued work needs an income shortfall and a real funded paid-time pathway.

steps.text: Check original age-sixty-six retirement income before deciding
Enrol if income short in funded paid-time training for posted bill-covering local lift-inspector role
Apply after qualifying if income short to posted bill-covering local inspector job with written stop-lift authority

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew thinking AI arrives in 2036 when I am sixty-eight and capable roof robots around 2039 when I am seventy-one. A 2039 roof robot should not leave a young rigger checking a damaged sling for free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would still want the younger crew to get paid safety checks, even if I am no longer on site. I would not promise a job at seventy-one when I have not even verified the retirement budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading paid panel work now and review our age-sixty-six income. If it covers our bills, I would retire at the original 2034 target and attend union meetings on safe robot lifts; if not, I would apply only to posted local lift-safety work with adequate wages and written stop-lift authority.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy until the budget is checked, yet calm about distant machines if it works. The longer horizon lets the crew negotiate paid inspections.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why attend meetings after you retire?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A damaged sling is dangerous whoever checks it. I can share my experience, while the younger members decide what agreement they need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you teach robot rigging for pay after 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if an actual posted local role existed with a suitable wage and safe authority. I would not promise to work after the retirement target without a household need.

say: The 2036 **thinking** change and 2039 robots may follow my original exit.
I would **still** support union terms for paid sling inspections.
think: **Work** after 2034 depends on a verified income shortfall.
**Any** later role requires a posted local vacancy, adequate wage and stop-lift authority.
do: **Retire** at original 2034 target only if verified household income covers bills.
**Attend** union meetings for paid robot-lift inspections after leaving regular site work.
**Apply** if retirement income falls short to posted local lift-safety work with bill-covering pay and written stop-lift authority.
feel: **Uneasy** until the household budget is verified, calmer about later robots.
S4.quote: A 2039 roof robot should not leave a young rigger checking a damaged sling for free.
fieldNote: Her **union** participation remains concrete even if paid site work ends at the original retirement target.
She does **not** presume a 2039 job; any later application needs a household income shortfall and safe adequate local work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast case worries me most because robots might cut roof-panel hours three years before my planned exit. An offered paid safety trial and a posted local inspector job with adequate pay and stop-lift authority would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who can order a robot lift stopped when a sling is damaged. The fastest machine on site still needs a person with paid time to look up and say no. A damaged sling does not become safe because the roof robot has a better schedule.

headlineQuote: A damaged sling does not become safe because the roof robot has a better schedule.
portrait: **Tara** is a fifty-eight-year-old trade-certified lead carpenter who fits timber roof panels.
Her **higher** pay, savings beyond six months, partner, grown children and many local builders provide options.
She **uses** AI daily, learns new controls early and seeks union terms for paid rigging checks.
She **hopes** to retire at sixty-six in 2034 if household income supports it; later work is conditional.
biggestWorry: **Fast** robots around 2031 could cut paid roof-panel work three years before her original target.
whatWouldHelp: An **offered** supervised paid trial and a posted local inspector role with household-covering pay and stop-lift authority would help.
